title: Client–Server & HTTP
subtitle: Request-response semantics, methods, status codes, and stateless scaling
objectives: Explain the request/response model and what's inside an HTTP request
Choose the right HTTP method and reason about safe retries with idempotency
Read status codes as signals about where a system is failing
Explain why stateless HTTP is what lets a service scale to thousands of servers

exercises.title: A client asks for work; a server performs it and responds
exercises.body: When a social app opens, your phone sends a *request* for the feed. A server reads data, applies the application's rules, and sends a *response*. In this conversation the phone is the client because it asks; the other machine is the server because it answers.
exercises.note: Client and server describe roles, not permanent machine types. An API server becomes a client when it asks a payment service to charge a card.

exercises.prompt: A page needs four resources from one origin. Reuse one HTTP/2 connection instead of opening four separate connections.
exercises.beforeStatus: CONNECTION SETUP · 4 TCP/TLS setups for 4 resources
exercises.afterStatus: CONNECTION REUSED · 1 TCP/TLS setup carries all 4 resource streams
exercises.why: HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple request streams over one connection to the same origin. Connection reuse removes repeated TCP and TLS setup; it does not remove each resource's request, response, or server work.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A page needs four resources from one origin. Reuse one HTTP/2 connection instead of opening four separate connections. Place Browser, Origin. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Browser → Origin. That topology is the evidence for the answer: HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple request streams over one connection to the same origin. Connection reuse removes repeated TCP and TLS setup; it does not remove each resource's request, response, or server work.

exercises.prompt: You open a social app and your feed appears. Where did that data physically come from the instant you opened it?
choices: It was already fully stored on your phone
Your phone asked a server, and the server answered
Another user's phone sent it straight to you
exercises.why: The phone acts as an HTTP client: it requests feed data from a server, which retrieves or computes the result and returns a response. This request/response boundary lets centrally managed services supply current data to many clients.

exercises.prompt: The machine that asks is the ______; the machine that answers is the server.
exercises.why: Client and server name roles in one interaction. The client initiates the request and the server answers it; the same process can become a client when it calls another service.

exercises.title: An HTTP request has a method, target, headers, and optional body
exercises.body: In `POST /users HTTP/1.1`, `POST` is the method and `/users` is the target path. Header lines such as `Content-Type: application/json` carry metadata. A blank line separates them from an optional body containing the new user's fields.
exercises.note: The method supplies operation semantics, the path selects a resource, headers describe the message, and the body carries a representation when needed.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of an HTTP request to its job.
exercises.why: The method states the operation, the path identifies the target resource, headers carry request metadata, and the optional body carries representation data. Together these fields give the server enough information to interpret an HTTP request.

exercises.prompt: Order one request/response round trip.
steps: Client sends it to the server
exercises.why: The client must construct and send a request before the server can process it. The server then constructs a response, and the client can render only after that response arrives.

exercises.prompt: You send one request, then another. By default, does the server remember your first request when handling the second?
choices: No — each HTTP request is independent (stateless)
Only if they're within one second
exercises.why: HTTP is stateless at the protocol level: one request does not implicitly provide memory of an earlier request. Applications preserve login state by sending a cookie or token with later requests and, when needed, resolving it against shared server-side state.

exercises.prompt: Which statement best captures what HTTP is?
choices: A database that stores your data
A stateless request/response protocol for clients and servers to talk
exercises.why: HTTP defines stateless request and response messages between clients and servers. It specifies message semantics and transport behavior for application communication; it is neither a database nor a programming language.

exercises.title: An HTTP method describes what the request intends to do
exercises.body: In `GET /users/42`, `GET` means read and `/users/42` identifies the resource. `POST` commonly creates, `PUT` replaces, and `DELETE` removes. The method and path together make the request's intent understandable to the server and to web infrastructure.
exercises.note: `GET` is safe when the client requests no application-state change, although the server may log or meter it. Destructive actions must not use `GET`, because browsers and crawlers may issue it automatically.

exercises.prompt: A mobile client retries `POST /charges` after a timeout. The first request already succeeded, so the retry creates a second charge. Give both attempts one operation identity.
choices: Retry with the same idempotency key
choiceFeedback: One operation identity lets the server recognize the duplicate attempt.
A longer timeout reduces some retries but cannot prove whether a timed-out charge succeeded.
A GET request cannot safely replace the command that creates the charge.
exercises.afterStatus: ONE TAP · 1 charge · retry returns stored result
exercises.result: The server recognized both requests as the same intended operation
exercises.why: The client reuses one idempotency key for every retry of the same charge. The server atomically reserves that key before performing work and returns the recorded result to later duplicates.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A mobile client retries `POST /charges` after a timeout. The first request already succeeded, so the retry creates a second charge. Give both attempts one operation identity. Place Charge API, Payments. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Client → Charge API; Charge API → Payments. That topology is the evidence for the answer: The client reuses one idempotency key for every retry of the same charge. The server atomically reserves that key before performing work and returns the recorded result to later duplicates.

exercises.prompt: You want to fetch a user's profile without changing anything. Which method?
exercises.why: `GET` expresses retrieval with safe semantics, meaning the requested operation should not change server state. Caches, crawlers, and prefetchers rely on that contract, so state-changing handlers should use a method whose semantics permit mutation.

exercises.prompt: Match each method to its intent.
exercises.why: `GET` retrieves a representation, `POST` submits data to create or process a subordinate resource, `PUT` replaces the resource at a known URI, and `DELETE` removes it. These method semantics make client intent explicit.

exercises.prompt: Which of these methods are expected to change state on the server? Select all.
exercises.why: `POST`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` can create, replace, or remove server state. `GET` is defined as safe and should perform retrieval without a requested state change.

exercises.prompt: Your `DELETE /users/42` request times out and you don't know if it worked. Is it safe to just send it again?
choices: Yes — deleting twice leaves the same result as deleting once
No — you might delete two different users
Only if you switch to `GET` first
exercises.why: `DELETE /users/42` is idempotent because repeating the same request leaves the target resource absent, the same intended state produced by one successful deletion. The server should still return an appropriate status when the resource is already gone.

exercises.prompt: Build a retry-safe payment path. The API claims the idempotency key first; only the winning request may call the payment processor.

nodes.sub: called by API after claim wins

exercises.why: The client repeats the same key. The Payment API atomically claims or reads that key in shared storage; only the request that wins the claim calls the Payment Processor, while later retries return the stored outcome. The store returns a decision to the API—it does not forward the charge itself. If reservation is not atomic across API servers, two retries can both charge the customer.

exercises.prompt: An operation is ______ if performing it many times has the same effect as performing it once.
exercises.why: An idempotent operation has the same intended effect after one execution or repeated executions. That property permits retries after ambiguous network failures without duplicating the state change.

lessons.title: Timeout retries can amplify an outage

exercises.title: A timeout often creates another request
exercises.body: If 8,000 original requests/sec produce retries for 75%, the server sees 14,000 attempts/sec. Extra work increases queueing and timeouts, which can trigger still more retries. Backoff spreads retries; a retry budget limits their total rate.
exercises.note: The server still needs idempotency because the first attempt and retry may both arrive.

exercises.prompt: Clients send 8,000 req/s. During slowness, 75% would retry once, but the service handles 10,000 attempts/sec. Drag the *smallest* share of retries prevented by budgets/backoff that keeps it alive.
exercises.why: With no suppression, retries raise load to 14,000 attempts/sec. Preventing 67% leaves about 9,980. Backoff spreads attempts in time; a retry budget caps how much extra work callers may create.

fieldTask.do: Right-click any page → Inspect → Network tab → reload
fieldTask.alt: Click any row to see its status code, method, and headers
fieldTask.notice: Inspect what actually appears after reload: `200` means a response body was returned; `304` means a cached copy was validated; 'memory cache' means no network body was needed; and a service worker may supply the response. DevTools can disable caching, so no one outcome is guaranteed.

exercises.title: The first digit groups HTTP responses by outcome
exercises.body: Read a status code by class first: `2xx` reports success; `3xx` covers redirection and related outcomes such as `304 Not Modified`; `4xx` means the request could not be fulfilled as sent; and `5xx` means the server failed while handling a valid request.
exercises.note: The classes guide behavior. Clients may correct a `4xx`; operators investigate rising `5xx`. They are not perfect blame labels—a valid request can still receive `404` or `429`.

exercises.prompt: A server replies with `200`. At a glance, what does that number tell you?
exercises.why: `200 OK` is an HTTP status code in the `2xx` success class, so it reports that the request succeeded. The first digit identifies the broad outcome class, while the remaining digits specify a particular result.

exercises.prompt: Match each status code to its meaning.
exercises.why: `200` reports success, `301` directs the client to a permanently moved resource, `404` reports an absent resource, and `500` reports an unexpected server failure. Accurate codes let clients and intermediaries handle each outcome correctly.

exercises.prompt: Which of these belong to the `4xx` client-error class? Select all.
exercises.why: `400`, `401`, and `404` all begin with 4 and therefore belong to the `4xx` request-error class. `503 Service Unavailable` belongs to `5xx` because the server is temporarily unable to serve the request.

exercises.prompt: Your service is getting hammered with more traffic than it can handle. Which status code politely tells clients to slow down?
exercises.why: `429 Too Many Requests` tells the client that a rate limit rejected the request. A `Retry-After` header or documented backoff policy can delay retries so clients do not immediately recreate the overload.

exercises.prompt: Your app sits behind a load balancer. Users start seeing `502` and `504` errors. Where is the problem most likely?
choices: Downstream of the load balancer — the app servers are failing or too slow
exercises.why: A gateway returns `502` when an upstream sends an invalid response and `504` when an upstream does not respond before the deadline. Both codes direct investigation toward the downstream application or its dependencies.

exercises.prompt: A user requests `GET /orders/99999`, but no such order exists. What should the server return?
exercises.why: `404 Not Found` accurately reports that the requested order resource does not exist. Returning `200` would send clients down a success path, while `500` would incorrectly classify an expected lookup result as a server fault.

exercises.title: Stateless servers keep request context out of one server's memory
exercises.body: A request must carry what any server needs to handle it, such as an authentication token or session ID. The application can still store users and orders in a database; *stateless* means one web server does not depend on private memory of the previous request.
exercises.note: Because any server can handle the next request, a load balancer can spread traffic freely and replace failed servers. Shared state still needs a database or cache.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: Stateless servers keep request context out of one server's memory
exercises.why: A request must carry what any server needs to handle it, such as an authentication token or session ID. The application can still store users and orders in a database; *stateless* means one web server does not depend on private memory of the previous request. Because any server can handle the next request, a load balancer can spread traffic freely and replace failed servers. Shared state still needs a database or cache.

exercises.prompt: A big service runs thousands of identical web servers behind one load balancer, and each of your requests may hit a different server — yet everything works. Why is that possible?
choices: The servers share one block of memory
HTTP is stateless, so any server can handle any request
Your requests secretly always hit the same server
The load balancer copies your data to every server
exercises.why: Each request carries the authentication and input needed to process it, so the load balancer can send it to any interchangeable server. Local session memory would create instance affinity and would lose the session when that instance failed.

exercises.prompt: If servers remember nothing between requests, where does your logged-in session actually live?
choices: In the client (a cookie/token it re-sends), or in a shared store like Redis
exercises.why: A client can carry a self-contained token, or it can carry a session identifier that every server resolves in a shared store. Both arrangements keep per-user session state out of individual app-server memory.

exercises.prompt: Place the missing piece so any app server can serve any request without losing the user's session.
exercises.why: A shared Redis cache makes the same session record available to both app servers. Because neither server depends on private session memory, either can handle the next request and either can be replaced independently.

exercises.title: Connection reuse amortizes setup across many HTTP requests
exercises.body: A fresh HTTPS connection can require transport and encryption handshakes before the first request. Keep-alive reuses that connection. HTTP/2 multiplexes concurrent streams over one TCP connection; HTTP/3 multiplexes QUIC streams over UDP.
exercises.note: With HTTP/2, one lost TCP packet can delay all streams waiting behind that byte gap. QUIC recovers loss per stream, avoiding that transport-level cross-stream block.

exercises.prompt: Opening a fresh TCP + TLS connection for every single request is expensive. Which of these reduce that cost? Select all.
choices: Keep-alive: reuse one connection for many requests
HTTP/2 multiplexing: many requests in flight on one connection
Opening a brand-new connection for every image
HTTP/3 over QUIC: avoids TCP-level head-of-line blocking
exercises.why: Keep-alive amortizes connection setup across requests, and multiplexing carries concurrent request streams on one connection. HTTP/3 uses independent QUIC streams, so loss on one stream does not impose TCP-level head-of-line blocking on the others.

exercises.title: Conditional requests validate a cached representation before resending it
exercises.body: A server can attach an entity tag (`ETag`) to a response. On a later request, the client sends that tag in `If-None-Match`. If the representation is unchanged, the server returns `304 Not Modified` without the response body; otherwise it returns the new body and tag.
exercises.note: `Cache-Control` decides when reuse or revalidation is allowed. An `ETag` identifies a representation version; it does not choose the caching policy by itself.

exercises.prompt: Your API serves a user avatar that rarely changes. How do you avoid re-sending the same bytes on every request?
choices: You can't — you must resend it each time
Use `Cache-Control` + an `ETag`: the client asks 'still current?' and the server can reply `304 Not Modified` with no body
Make the image smaller each time
exercises.why: An `ETag` identifies a specific representation version. The client sends it in a conditional request, and the server returns `304 Not Modified` without the avatar body when that version is still current, saving transfer bytes while retaining validation.

exercises.prompt: A bank must revoke a stolen device within 5 seconds. Authentication must fail closed if revocation state is unavailable, and the service handles 20,000 authenticated requests/sec. Which design meets the requirement?
choices: A self-contained token valid for 24 hours, with no server-side revocation check
An opaque session ID checked against a replicated shared store on each request, with capacity for 20,000 checks/sec
A self-contained token valid for 1 hour, checked only when it expires
A cookie stored only in one app server's memory
exercises.why: Checking an opaque session ID against replicated shared state lets a revocation become visible within the 5-second target and lets the service reject requests when that state is unavailable. The store must be provisioned for 20,000 checks/sec. Long-lived self-contained tokens without a revocation check cannot meet the stated deadline.

exercises.prompt: Users randomly get logged out, but only during high traffic. The setup: app servers store sessions in their own local memory, behind a round-robin load balancer. What's happening, and what's the fix?
choices: DNS is misconfigured — flush the cache
Round-robin sends you to servers that don't have your in-memory session → move sessions to a shared store so servers are stateless
The database ran out of disk — add storage
The users' tokens expired — shorten the timeout
exercises.why: Round-robin routing sends requests to instances that lack the user’s locally stored session, causing intermittent authentication loss. Moving sessions to a shared store restores server interchangeability; sticky routing only masks the dependency and still fails when the pinned instance disappears.

exercises.prompt: A photo client times out after sending `PUT /avatars/42` with the complete replacement image. Under an idempotent endpoint contract, what is the safest retry?
choices: Change to POST and create another avatar
exercises.why: Repeating the same complete replacement converges on the same resource state. The timeout does not reveal whether the first request succeeded, so retry safety comes from the endpoint's idempotent replacement semantics.
